abstract.p: Antiviral peptides (AVPs) hold great potential for combating viral infections, yet their discovery and development remain challenging. In this study, we present a hybrid model combining Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks to address these challenges. The BiLSTM model was thoroughly constructed and validated, showing reliable performance in identifying AVPs. Additionally, analyses such as applicability domain and feature importance from BiLSTM provided valuable insights into the generated peptides. The performance of the WGAN-GP model was comprehensively evaluated, confirming its ability to produce diverse and functional peptide sequences. The model successfully generated and identified 815 novel AVPs, demonstrating its effectiveness in peptide generation and classification. Novel antiviral peptides (AVPs) were successfully identified across all viral endpoints tested. However, their abundance exhibited significant variability, with the highest levels observed in influenza A virus and the lowest levels detected in human parainfluenza virus type 3. These findings highlight the potential of our hybrid approach as a powerful tool for antiviral peptide discovery and contribute to advancing peptide-based therapeutic research. To maximize its impact on AVPs discovery, we have deployed our predictive models as a publicly accessible platform at https://avp-predictor.streamlit.app, offering researchers a practical tool for prioritizing candidate peptides.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Infectious diseases, particularly viral infections, ranked among the most formidable public health challenges worldwide, marked by their rapid transmission, extensive spread, and devastating impact on human well-being. A 2020 analysis by the Institute of Labor Economics, a German nonprofit organization, revealed the staggering global economic cost of eight major diseases—HIV/AIDS, malaria, measles, hepatitis, dengue, rabies, tuberculosis, and yellow fever—estimated at an astonishing US$8 trillion. In 2016 alone, these diseases resulted in the loss of over 156 million years of life. Based on this report, it is evident that seven out of the eight diseases analyzed are attributed to viral infections1, highlighting the critical urgency for innovative and effective strategies to combat this evolving global health threat.

Viral infections continue to impose immense health and socioeconomic burdens worldwide, with the concept of viral infectious diseases of poverty (VIDP) shedding light on viral illnesses disproportionately affecting populations in low- and middle-income countries. These diseases thrive in the context of poverty, fueled by inadequate healthcare systems, poor sanitation, malnutrition, and limited access to preventive measures2. Recent analyses, leveraging data from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 20213, have provided critical insights into the global impact of six major VIDPs: COVID-19, HIV/AIDS, acute hepatitis, dengue, rabies, and Ebola virus disease (EVD). In 2021, VIDPs were responsible for an estimated 8.7 million deaths and approximately 259.2 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). These figures represent 12.8% of global deaths and 9.0% of the total global burden of all-cause DALYs, underscoring the significant impact of VIDPs on global health3.

Based on comprehensive data collected and analyzed from 1990 to 2021, three viral infectious diseases with significant global health impacts stand out: COVID-19, HIV/AIDS, and dengue fever. Among these, COVID-19 has been the most devastating, accounting for approximately 7.9 million deaths and 212.0 million DALYs. HIV/AIDS remains a critical concern, with deaths and DALYs increasing by 134.7% and 115.6%, respectively, compared to 1990 levels. Dengue fever has shown alarming trends, with deaths nearly doubling from 14,315 in 1990 to 29,076 in 2021, alongside a notable rise in incidence and prevalence. Conversely, acute hepatitis and rabies have shown a marked improvement, with DALYs decreasing by 57.0% and 58.4%, respectively, over the same period. The burden of EVD remains the lowest among the diseases studied, with only 48 deaths and 2,602 DALYs reported in 20213.

The threat of increased antiviral resistance and the health risk of emerging infectious diseasess endorses further research into novel antiviral compounds. Recently, peptide-based drugs have been proposed as they have lower cost, possess good tolerability, are relatively safe, and are highly selective4,5. Among these peptide-based drugs, antiviral peptides (AVPs) have great significance in the development of novel drugs. AVPs are a sub-class of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) that also work as antimicrobial in addition to antiviral activities6,7. AVPs have been shown to affect the viral replication cycle through several mechanisms: by perturbing the membranes of enveloped viruses; inhibiting cellular penetration or intracellular trafficking; restricting viral transcription and translation; and/or preventing budding of mature viral particles8,9. Several AVPs are currently patented and approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use against the HIV, influenza virus, and hepatitis virus, demonstrating the efficacy of these robust therapeutic alternatives10. AVPs present numerous benefits, yet the availability of comprehensive data on these peptides remains notably constrained. Although extensive repositories of natural and synthetic AMPs are available, including APD3, DRAMP 2.0, CAMP-R3, dbAMP, and ADAM, only a small portion of their entries specifically document antiviral activity11–15. Moreover, databases exclusively dedicated to AVPs, such as AVPdb16 and HIPdb17, are rare. Although these databases collectively house thousands to over 29,000 unique peptides, AVPs account for only 1–7% of the total entries9. This highlights an urgent need for more novel data sets to drive progress in AVPs research. Enhancing the novel AVPs could improve AVP identification, optimize therapy, and advance antiviral drug development.

Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have driven the development of sophisticated machine learning tools for the discovery of AVPs directly from their primary sequences. By leveraging deep learning (DL) methodologies, these tools have become highly effective in decoding sequence-level information and generating novel AVPs18,19. In this study, we present a hybrid generative deep neural network framework combining Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP)20 and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks21–23. This innovative approach is designed to both generate and identify potential AVPs with high precision, offering a powerful avenue for the discovery of new therapeutic agents. Key highlights of our research are as follows:
We constructed a BiLSTM model utilizing sequence-derived fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors to facilitate the prediction of newly generated AVP sequences. Additionally, an in-depth analysis was performed to pinpoint amino acid residues that significantly impact the model’s predictive accuracy. A rigorous evaluation of the applicability domain covering 12 viral endpoints was also undertaken, offering a well-founded basis for the classification of AVPs specific to different viruses.
We employed a WGAN-GP model to drive innovation in peptide generation, yielding 300 novel sequences. We conducted comprehensive assessments to compare the diversity and similarity of amino acid compositions between the generated and original data sets, ensuring high-quality outputs suitable for subsequent predictive modeling.
We synergistically combined the WGAN-GP and BiLSTM architectures in a hybrid framework, achieving precise classification of AVPs across distinct viral endpoints. We used this approach to significantly enrich the data set and deepen insights into the AVP properties.
We identified key regions of sequence similarity between the original and generated data sets through local pairwise sequence alignment using the Smith-Waterman algorithm, facilitating the recognition of functional similarities. We systematically examined conserved motifs crucial for antiviral activity in the generated peptides, underscoring their potential functional relevance.

sec.title: Experimental procedures
Data set preparation
sec.p: To build the BiLSTM model for predicting the antiviral activity of newly generated peptides, the data sets were carefully selected from a previous study24 and established repositories to ensure high-quality and reliable inputs. Specifically, AVP sequences were extracted from comprehensive databases, including dbAMP11, AVPdb16, DRAMP13, and HIPdb17. Sequences containing invalid amino acids were systematically excluded to maintain data integrity, resulting in a final data set comprising 5,220 unique AVP sequences targeting a diverse range of viral strains. For generating negative samples, non-AVP sequences without virus-specific activity were sourced from dbAMP11, DBAASP25, and DRAMP13, yielding a data set of 1,776 non-AVPs. This rigorously curated data set (referred to as Database A) provides a robust foundation for model training and comprehensive performance evaluation across multiple viral endpoints using the BiLSTM architecture.

In addition, a specialized data set (designated as Database B) was derived exclusively from AVPdb16 and ADPDB database26 which are trusted repositories of experimentally validated AVPs targeting clinically relevant viruses. This data set includes AVPs associated with the 12 viruses having the highest number of validated entries, enabling a focused analysis of peptide efficacy. Using this data set, the BiLSTM models was developed to evaluate the model’s virus-specific predictive performance for each viral endpoint, offering insights into targeted peptide efficacy against clinically significant viral infections. Virus types, abbreviations, and sequence statistics were summarized in Supplementary Table S1.

To prevent information leakage, we removed sequences that were exactly identical between the training and test sets. However, we did not apply additional redundancy reduction methods such as CD-HIT, as our focus was on preserving sequence order. Peptides with similar or identical amino acid composition may differ in residue arrangement, which can significantly influence their biological function and the model’s ability to learn meaningful patterns. Therefore, we retained non-identical sequences to maintain diversity, while eliminating only exact duplicates.

sec.title: Feature representation of amino acid sequence
sec.p: To construct the BiLSTM-based predictive model, we incorporated five categories of sequence-based features, ensuring comprehensive input representation. These feature categories include: (1) amino acid composition28 (AAC), which captures the overall residue distribution; (2) the K-mer method29(K_mer), encoding subsequence patterns of length k; (3) one-hot encoding29 (One_hot), a binary representation of each amino acid; (4) 14 physicochemical descriptors30 (Phychem) encompassing critical sequence properties such as length, hydrophobicity, molecular weight, isoelectric point, aromaticity, instability index, flexibility, grand average of hydropathicity (GRAVY), net charge at pH 7.4, and secondary structure fractions (helix, turn, sheet), as well as cysteine reduction and disulfide bridge counts; and (5) sequence tokens29 (Seq_Tokens), capturing positional information and contextual sequence elements.

A comprehensive computational framework for protein sequence analysis is implemented using a combination of robust Python libraries. AAC is derived utilizing pandas and native Python functions for efficient residue frequency computation. K-mer fingerprints are extracted using scikit-learn (v1.5.2)’s CountVectorizer, enabling feature-based sequence representation. One-hot encoding is efficiently applied via NumPy (v.1.26.4), ensuring precise numerical encoding of amino acid sequences. To capture physicochemical properties, Biopython (v1.82)’s Bio.SeqUtils.ProtParam module is employed, leveraging the ProteinAnalysis class to compute key properties such as isoelectric point, aromaticity, instability index, flexibility, GRAVY, net charge, and secondary structure fractions. Additionally, bespoke Python dictionaries enable precise estimations of hydrophobicity and molecular weight, while cysteine-associated attributes, including the prediction of potential disulfide bridge formations, are systematically inferred through direct sequence analysis. For sequence tokenization, TensorFlow Keras (v2.17.0)’s Tokenizer is utilized at the character level, converting amino acid sequences into structured numeric representations, essential for deep learning-based sequence modeling.

sec.title: BiLSTM network for AVPs prediction
sec.p: The BiLSTM models were constructed using a stacked architecture comprising two BiLSTM layers with 64 and 32 cell units in the first and second layers, respectively. These layers were followed by a fully connected neural network (FCNN) layer with 100 neurons and a ReLU activation function, designed to capture and enhance key features from the BiLSTM outputs. The output layer included a single neuron with a sigmoid activation function, applying a threshold of 0.5 for binary classification. The models were trained using the ADAM optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001, and binary cross-entropy was used as the loss function. The data set was partitioned into training and validation subsets in a 7:3 ratio, consistent with other applied methodologies. Each model was trained for 50 epochs, and the overall model construction is depicted in Fig. 1B.

These BiLSTM architectures were employed to develop predictive models for the comprehensive data set as well as for specialized subsets corresponding to 12 distinct viral endpoints. Model performance was rigorously assessed using established metrics including balanced accuracy (BACC), the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), precision, sensitivity, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC)31,32. For performance acceptance, a BiLSTM model should has an MCC value greater than 0.5, with an optimal target approaching 1, indicating a robust concordance between predicted and actual outcomes33. The optimal BiLSTM model, demonstrating superior predictive performance, was selected to evaluate feature importance and applicability domain (AD) before assessing the antiviral potential of novel AVP candidates generated by the WGAN-GP framework for each specific viral endpoint.

sec.title: WGAN-GP framework
sec.p: In this study, we utilized the WGAN-GP framework to improve the stability and quality of the generative model34. Unlike standard GANs, which employ the Jensen–Shannon divergence to measure the difference between the original and generated data distributions, WGAN-GP leverages the Wasserstein-1 distance (also known as the Earth Mover’s Distance) and penalizes the gradient norm of the critic. This metric provides a more meaningful measure of divergence, resulting in smoother gradients and improved convergence during training.

In this framework, the generator model receives a random noise vector of size 300, sampled from a normal distribution, as an input. This noise vector is processed through three FCNN layers to produce synthetic amino acid sequences. The first layer consists of 512 units with a leaky ReLU activation function, followed by a second layer with 1,024 units and a leaky ReLU activation. The final layer uses a tanh activation function. The output is reshaped into a one-hot encoded sequence representing the generated amino acid chain. The generator is trained to map random noise inputs to realistic outputs, producing sequences that closely resemble original amino acid sequences (Fig. 1C, generator network).

The critic model functionally resembling a discriminator in conventional GANs processes the input through a structured sequence of two FCNN layers where the first layer consists of 512 neurons with ReLU activation and the second layer consists of 256 neurons with ReLU activation to capture complex feature representations effectively. The final output layer consists of a single unit with a linear activation, producing a scalar value that represents the Wasserstein distance score (Fig. 1C, critic network). This distance score helps distinguish original sequences from generated ones, guiding the generator to improve over successive iterations.

sec.title: WGAN-WP training procedure
sec.p: The WGAN-GP model is trained by updating the critic multiple times per generator update. Specifically, for each epoch, the critic is updated 5 times for every single update of the generator, ensuring that it provides an accurate estimate of the Wasserstein distance. The critic’s loss function is designed to minimize the difference between the critic’s outputs for original and generated data, with an additional gradient penalty term to enforce the Lipschitz constraint. The generator, on the other hand, is trained by minimizing the negative output of the critic, encouraging it to produce data that the critic classifies as original. Both models are optimized using the Adam optimizer, with different learning rates for the generator (0.0002) and the critic (0.0001), and hyperparameters set to 0.5 and 0.9 for the first and second momentum terms, respectively.

Upon completing the training phase, the WGAN-GP model generated 300 novel amino acid sequences. Each sequence was reconstructed by decoding the one-hot encoded representations, determining the amino acid with the highest probability at each position. The resulting sequences were stored for subsequent analysis. In the next step, the validated BiLSTM model was utilized to evaluate the antiviral potential of the generated sequences. This predictive analysis led to the identification of AVPs with activity against 12 human viruses, providing valuable insights into potential therapeutic candidates.

In addition, the methodologies for feature importance of BiLSTM model, AD analysis of BiLSTM model, Shannon entropy assessment of amino acid sequence diversity, pairwise Hamming distance distribution of structural variability, similarity analysis of amino acid composition, local pairwise sequence alignment using Smith-Waterman algorithm and conserved motif identification are described in the Supporting Information.

sec.title: Deployment of the AVP predictor as a web server
sec.p: To provide a user-friendly interface for the practical use of our AVP prediction models, we implemented a web server using the Streamlit framework (v1.35.0) in Python 3.10. The backend supports both the general AVP prediction model and twelve virus-specific BiLSTM models, which were previously trained and saved in .keras format using TensorFlow 2.11.0. Each model is paired with a corresponding pre-processing pipeline stored as .pkl files, which includes standardized amino acid sequence cleaning and fixed-length 3-mer fingerprint extraction.

The application loads pre-trained models during initialization and uses in-memory caching to improve responsiveness. Input peptide sequences, whether submitted individually or uploaded as a CSV file, are processed through a unified K-mer encoding pipeline before being fed into the selected BiLSTM model. Outputs include binary labels and prediction scores, with batch results available for download. The web server was deployed via Streamlit Cloud, which directly integrates with a public GitHub repository. All predictions are processed in real time within the app container, with no user data stored server-side.

sec.title: Results
Sequence feature distribution between antiviral and non-antiviral peptides
sec.p:
We first looked at the sequence feature distribution across various sequence fingerprints and descriptors between antiviral and non-antiviral peptides, using unsupervised t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) algorithm (Fig. 2). Our results indicated that sequence representations such as AAC, K-mer, one-hot encoding, and sequence tokens demonstrated clearer separability between these groups (Fig. 2A-D), as reflected by more distinct clusters and reduced overlap. In contrast, physicochemical descriptors exhibited limited separation between AVPs and non-AVPs (Fig. 2E), as evidenced by overlapping regions and small inter-cluster distances in the resulting plots. This no difference in clustering patterns highlights the potential utility of sequence-based features in predictive modeling. Consequently, we conducted a further analysis to assess how these sequence representations influence the performance of the BiLSTM models.Fig. 2
Sequence features distribution of the data set using (A) AAC fingerprints. (B) K-mer (K=3) fingerprints. (C) One-hot encoded fingerprints. (D) Sequence tokens. (E) Physicochemical descriptors.

sec.title: Overall performance of BiLSTM models on the AVPs test set
sec.p:
We utilized all of those five peptide representations to build the BiLSTM model for classifying AVPs and non-AVPs. The results presented in the heatmap reveal notable differences in the performance of models based on the Phychem, AAC, Seq_Tokens, K-mer (K=3), and One-hot encoding features. We found that the Phychem demonstrated the weakest performance across all evaluation metrics as illustrated in Fig. 3. Specifically, model with Phychem yielded an AUC of 0.500 and an MCC of 0.000, indicating that it lacked predictive power and failed to distinguish between the two groups effectively. Although it achieved a sensitivity of 1.000, this result is misleading, as the poor MCC and low F1 Score suggest that the model likely overfitted or produced biased predictions. Additionally, it should be noted that the Phychem feature set yields BACC and AUC values of 0.5, suggesting limited predictive power for AVP classification when used independently. Nevertheless, features with limited standalone performance can still offer complementary insights or serve as reference points. Furthermore, as our best-performing model is based on non-Phychem features, we retained Phychem in the comparative analysis to ensure completeness and transparency.Fig. 3
Predictive performance of BiLSTM models using various sequence-based features. These results are expressed from the mean of three independent experiments. (A) BACC, (B) Sensitivity, (C) MCC, (D) AUROC, (E) Precision, and (F) F1 score. Accuracy and sensitivity values >= 0.8, MCC values >= 0.5, and AUROC, Precision and F1 scores >= 0.9 were highlighted in red.

In contrast, AAC showed moderate performance, with BACC of 0.777, AUC of 0.863, and an F1 score of 0.877. While AAC performed significantly better than Phychem, its MCC value of 0.533 remained relatively low, implying that the model struggled to produce consistently accurate predictions. Moreover, the AAC feature was notably inferior compared to other sequence-based feature representations such as Seq_Tokens or K-mer (K=3), indicating that this feature is not the best peptide representation for classifying AVPs. On the other hand, the performance of Seq_Tokens was substantially better than that of Phychem and AAC, with an AUC of 0.899, a precision of 0.930, and an F1 score of 0.903. The MCC value of 0.643 indicated that models using Seq_Tokens produced more balanced predictions, though it slightly lagged behind the top-performing models. This result suggests that Seq_Tokens is a viable feature representation, offering a good balance between complexity and predictive power.

The best performance was achieved by models using K-mer and One-hot encoding, which exhibited near-identical results across all metrics. Both feature representations achieved high AUC values of 0.919 and 0.900, respectively, along with precision scores exceeding 0.940 and F1 scores over 0.900. Their MCC values were 0.685 for K-mer and 0.674 for One-hot encoding, highlighting their robustness and reliability in making accurate predictions. The superior clustering and separation achieved by K-mer and One-hot encoding likely contributed to their high predictive accuracy, making them the most effective feature representations in this study.

Among all the evaluated feature representations, K-mer demonstrated the highest overall performance, consistently yielding superior outcomes across key evaluation metrics. Notably, the model employing K-mer achieved BACC of 0.861, MCC of 0.685, an AUC of 0.919, precision of 0.946, and F1 score of 0.916, indicating its robust discriminative ability and predictive accuracy for AVPs. These results were obtained using a comprehensive data set comprising both within- and out-of-domain sequences. BiLSTM, an advanced variant of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), is highly effective in sequence modeling due to its ability to capture bidirectional context—integrating information from both preceding and succeeding elements in a sequence. Its LSTM units excel at managing long-range dependencies, overcoming the limitations of standard RNNs. The K-mer representation further enhances sequence analysis by partitioning sequences into overlapping subsequences of fixed length k, thereby preserving local patterns and motifs. By learning from these K-mers, BiLSTM not only captures intricate local features but also leverages global context, resulting in a more comprehensive sequence representation and superior predictive performance. These findings demonstrate that the BiLSTM model effectively captures the majority of sequence representations, providing a solid groundwork for its utilization in future in-depth experimental explorations.

sec.title: Comparison of the BiLSTM with other existing AVP prediction tools
sec.p:
We conducted a comprehensive performance evaluation of our BiLSTM model using K-mer fingerpints by comparing it with several well-established models on data set closely aligned with our study. These benchmark models include Guan et al method24, Chang et al method36, PreTP-Stack37, DeepAVP38, AVPpred39, iAMPpred40, and Meta-iAVP41. The BiLSTM model outperforms several methods in various metrics. Specifically, BiLSTM achieves higher accuracy (0.874) and MCC (0.685) than iAMPpred (accuracy: 0.817, MCC: 0.62) and Meta-iAVP (accuracy: 0.807, MCC: 0.6). The BiLSTM also performed had higher accuracy than AVPpred (accuracy: 0.857). Furthermore, BiLSTM demonstrates superior specificity (0.834) compared to these two models, with iAMPpred and Meta-iAVP reporting specificity scores of 0.705 and 0.773, respectively. Notably, BiLSTM’s sensitivity (0.887) also exceeds that of Meta-iAVP (0.833), highlighting its better performance in correctly identifying positive instances.

While BiLSTM delivers competitive results, it does not outperform certain top-performing models. Guan et al method exhibits the best overall performance, with an accuracy of 0.942, MCC of 0.88, sensitivity of 0.933, and specificity of 0.955, significantly surpassing BiLSTM in all metrics. Similarly, PreTP-Stack and Change et al achieve higher accuracy (0.894 and 0.895, respectively) and MCC (0.79 and 0.79, respectively) than BiLSTM. DeepAVP also outperforms BiLSTM in both accuracy (0.876) and MCC (0.75), though the difference in sensitivity is less pronounced (0.9 for DeepAVP versus 0.887 for BiLSTM). These results indicate that the BiLSTM also need a room further optimization. Nevertheless, the BiLSTM outperforms iAMPpred and Meta-iAVP across all key evaluation metrics, demonstrating its superior predictive performance over these models. Although AVPpred achieves a slightly higher MCC (0.71) compared to BiLSTM (0.685), BiLSTM exhibits marginally better sensitivity (0.887 vs. 0.883) and specificity (0.834 vs. 0.822), resulting in a more balanced overall performance. Despite falling short of top-performing models such as Guan et al, PreTP-Stack, and Chang et al, BiLSTM’s high sensitivity (0.887) and balanced specificity (0.834) make it a competitive alternative. Consequently, we utilized the BiLSTM for subsequent detailed analyses.

sec.title: Permutation feature importance of amino acids
sec.p: Permutation feature importance is a robust, model-agnostic method for quantifying the contribution of individual features to model performance42. By randomly permuting the values of a feature and measuring the resulting decrease in accuracy, this approach provides an unbiased estimate of feature relevance. Since it is independent of the model architecture, it can be applied to a wide range of machine learning models, making it particularly valuable for interpreting complex models43. In this study, feature importance scores were calculated based on the average accuracy drop observed across 30 random shuffles of each feature. The BiLSTM model utilizing K-mer fingerprints is further applied in this experiment.

As a representation of amino acid sequences in the best-performing models, we analyzed permutation feature importance using K-mer fingerprints. The results identified Feature No. 1456 as having the highest importance score (0.0035), as illustrated in Fig. 4A. Subsequently, we filtered a list of sequences containing this feature. Based on this selection, we further identified the most influential amino acids affecting the AVPs prediction model.

Next, we determined the crucial amino acid residues that exert the greatest influence on predictive outcomes. Figure 4B illustrates the importance scores of individual amino acids in influencing the performance of the AVPs prediction model. Among the listed amino acids, phenylalanine (F) exhibits the highest importance score (0.1778), indicating that it plays a crucial role in distinguishing AVPs. Following cysteine (C) (0.1540), leucine (L) (0.1333) and isoleucine (0.1143) also contribute significantly to the predictive accuracy of the model. Other amino acids, such as alanine (0.0397), histidine (H) (0.0381) and proline (P) (0.0349), display moderate importance, suggesting that these residues may be involved in key structural or functional motifs of AVPs. Meanwhile, threonine (T) (0.0286, glutamic acid (E) (0.0222), and arginine (R) (0.0222) contribute to the model with slightly lower importance scores, implying that they are less critical for distinguishing antiviral peptides in the data sets used.

Overall, the analysis highlights that a subset of amino acids, particularly phenylalanine (F), cysteine (C), and leucine (L), are three key contributors to the prediction model’s performance. This information can be leveraged to better understand the structural features of AVPs and improve future predictive models by focusing on these important residues.Fig. 4

sec.title: Virus-specific predictive performance of BiLSTM models on test set
sec.p: To ensure accuracy in predicting AVPs for each viral endpoint, we employed a BiLSTM model for 12 distinct viral endpoints, utilizing all five sequence representations—specifically, AAC, K-mer, one-hot encoding, sequence tokens, and physicochemical descriptors. This resulted in the development of 60 BiLSTM-based models. The results demonstrate that different sequence representations yield varying predictive performance across the viral endpoints. The highest predictive performance for each virus type along with its corresponding sequence representation is illustrated in Fig. 5A. The findings reveal that K-mer fingerprints achieve the best performance for six viral endpoints, including HCV, HSV1, RSV, INFVA, HPIV3, and FIV, with the balanced accuracy scores ranging from 0.662 to 0.971. Specifically, the MCC, AUC, and F1 score values span from 0.406 to 0.945, 0.798 to 0.972, and 0.736 to 0.970, respectively. Among these, HPIV3 achieves the highest precision at 1.000, whereas INFVA has the lowest at 0.595. Conversely, INFVA attains the highest sensitivity at 0.965, while HSV1 registers the lowest at 0.756.

Likewise, one-hot encoding proves to be the most effective method for DENV2, SNV, and HBV, attaining balanced accuracy scores between 0.848 and 0.981. The MCC, AUC, and F1 score values range from 0.698 to 0.965, 0.903 to 0.999, and 0.866 to 0.981, respectively. Among these, SNV demonstrates the highest precision and sensitivity at 0.991 and 0.971, whereas DENV2 records the lowest values at 0.858 and 0.875, respectively.

Meanwhile, AAC fingerprints excel in predicting SARS, ANDV, and VACV, with balanced accuracy score ranging from 0.651 to 0.994. The MCC, AUC, and F1 score values range from 0.349 to 0.877, 0.595 to 1, and 0.723 to 0.994, respectively. Among these, ANDV exhibits the highest precision and sensitivity, reaching 1 and 0.987, respectively, while SARS shows the lowest values at 0.610 and 0.889.

These results indicate that the BiLSTM can effectively classify virus-specific AVPs. Subsequently, models utilizing the corresponding sequence features were tested for their AD for each virus before being employed in virus-specific predictions, ensuring that this approach lays a robust foundation for the prediction of newly generated sequences.Fig. 5

sec.title: Applicability domain to BiLSTM for each viral endpoint
sec.p: This study uses an AD analysis employing a Euclidean distance-based kNN algorithm, selected for its computational simplicity and capability to effectively characterize local neighborhood structures in the feature space21. The primary objective was to distinguish in-domain sequences from outliers across 12 data sets, each representing a distinct viral endpoint. By systematically varying the number of neighbors (k) from 2 to 10, we determined the optimal k-value for each data set by balancing two criteria: minimizing the number of excluded sequences and maximizing model performance. This approach facilitated the exclusion of out-of-domain sequences, ensuring a more homogeneous input space.

After refining the AD, the BiLSTM model was re-evaluated on filtered test sets using the identified fingerprints as input features. Supplementary Table S2 shows performance improvement of viral endpoint classification after AD refinement demonstrates varying trends across different metrics and viral endpoints.

BACC improvements varied considerably across all endpoints. SARS achieves the highest improvement at +12.77%, indicating a substantial gain in balanced classification performance. FIV (+8.20%) and DENV2 (+2.58%) also show moderate gains, while endpoints like VACV (+0.46%) and RSV (+0.50%) exhibit smaller improvements. MCC values reflect notable performance gains for FIV (+20.60%) and SARS (+9.70%), highlighting improved correlation between predicted and actual classifications for these endpoints. HSV1 (+6.40%) and HCV (+4.10%) also show meaningful improvements, while endpoints like VACV (+0.41%) and HBV (+0.08%) exhibit minimal changes. SNV shows an almost negligible change of +0.01%. Similarly, AUC values improve notably for SARS (+11.15%) and DENV2 (+4.92%), indicating enhanced overall ranking quality for these endpoints. Moderate gains are observed for SNV (+3.59%) and HPIV3 (+2.00%), while most other endpoints exhibit more modest gains or no change (e.g., ANDV and VACV).

In addition, precision improves dramatically for SARS (+54.01%), signifying a significant reduction in false positives for this endpoint. DENV2 (+6.18%) and HSV1 (+5.20%) also see noteworthy gains, while some endpoints, such as FIV (−5.70%) and INFVA (−2.20%), show decreases in precision. Moreover, SARS achieves the highest sensitivity improvement at +10.88%, followed by FIV (+6.50%) and HCV (+3.40%). Moderate increases are observed for endpoints such as HPIV3 (+3.10%) and SNV (+2.99%). Lastly, the F1 score, which balances precision and sensitivity, shows the most significant improvement for SARS (+12.53%), followed by DENV2 (+2.36%) and HCV (+2.20%). Smaller improvements are observed for endpoints like HPIV3 and HSV1 (+1.50%) and SNV (+1.96%), while INFVA shows a decline of −1.10%. These results highlight that while AD refinement substantially enhances performance for certain viral endpoints, particularly SARS, DENV2, and FIV, the impact varies significantly across metrics and endpoints.

Building on the performance improvement results, we provide a comprehensive summary of the BiLSTM model’s performance on in-domain sequences for each viral endpoint, highlighting the proportion of outliers removed for different k values, as visualized in Fig. 5B. A clear enhancement is observed in Fig. 5B (which includes only in-domain entries) compared to Fig. 5A (which includes both in-domain and out-of-domain entries) across all endpoints. However, there are striking differences in the extent of outlier removal. Notably, FIV and SARS exhibit the highest removal rates at 48.44% and 22.03%, respectively, while HSV1 records a significantly lower proportion at just 2.22%. These findings underscore the models differential handling of outliers across viral endpoints, highlighting the variability in its performance.

sec.title: Sequence distribution of original and generated data set
sec.p: Concurrently, we employed the WGAN-GP model with carefully tuned hyperparameters to generate 300 novel sequences. The distribution of sequences generated by the WGAN-GP model was compared with the original data using two dimensionality reduction techniques: t-SNE and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). t-SNE and UMAP are powerful nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques that have become essential for visualizing complex chemical spaces44,45. In this study, t-SNE was selected for its remarkable ability to capture intricate local structures and uncover hidden patterns within high-dimensional chemical data, which is crucial for accurately representing molecular relationships. Additionally, prior research has demonstrated t-SNE’s superior performance in preserving nearest neighbors, further reinforcing its suitability for this task. On the other hand, UMAP offers a more balanced approach by preserving both local and global structures, addressing a limitation of t-SNE44. This makes UMAP an increasingly recognized method for dimensionality reduction, as it effectively retains the overall structure of the data in lower-dimensional representations46,47. Consequently, both t-SNE and UMAP are valuable techniques for analyzing molecular relationships, distinguishing chemical clusters, and enhancing the interpretability of chemical space visualizations.

Figure 6 presents a comparative analysis of the original and generated data sets using t-SNE and UMAP visualizations across three sequence features: amino acid composition, K-mer fingerprints, and one-hot encoded fingerprints. Across all three features, a significant degree of overlap is observed between the original (blue) and generated (red) data sets, reflecting the generative model’s ability to replicate the overall characteristics of the original data. However, deviations are consistently present in all features, with some generated data points lying outside the main clusters of the original data set. In the t-SNE plots, amino acid composition (Fig. 6A), K-mer fingerprints (Fig. 6B), and one-hot encoded fingerprints (Fig. 6C) all show overlap, but each also exhibits varying degrees of scattered points outside the core clusters, indicating systematic differences. Similarly, in the UMAP plots, amino acid composition (Fig. 6D), K-mer fingerprints (Fig. 6E), and one-hot encoded fingerprints (Figure 6F) demonstrate alignment with the original data, while scattered points outside the main clusters reveal deviations in all three features. These observations highlight the generative model’s strength in capturing the general characteristics of the data while emphasizing the need for further refinement to address the deviations across all features. The combined t-SNE and UMAP analyses provide a comprehensive evaluation, revealing both the strengths and the areas requiring improvement in the generative approach.Fig. 6

sec.p:

Shannon entropy distribution is presented in Fig. 7A. The histogram depicts the entropy values of individual sequences in the original (blue) and generated (orange) AVPs. Both distributions exhibit a similar pattern, with their mean entropy values of 3.05 and 3.03 for the original and generated sequences, respectively. This close alignment of mean entropy suggests that the generated sequences maintain a comparable level of randomness and complexity to the original sequences, indicating the model’s capability to preserve essential sequence characteristics.Fig. 7

Figure 7B shows the violin plot of pairwise diversity distribution for sequences in the original and generated AVPs. While the generated sequences (mean diversity = 0.64) exhibit slightly higher pairwise diversity compared to the original sequences (mean diversity = 0.66), the overall shape of the distributions indicates a reasonable similarity. The increased diversity in the generated sequences implies that the model not only captures the diversity present in the original AVPs but also introduces novel variations, potentially broadening the sequence space. These findings collectively indicate that the WGAN-GP model effectively generates sequences that are structurally similar to the original AVPs while enhancing sequence diversity, a desirable trait for applications involving exploration of novel sequence spaces.

sec.p:

While slight variations are observed, particularly at the peak density and tail regions (highlighted in arrows), these differences remain minimal, indicating that the generated data set effectively captures the key statistical properties of the original sequences. sec.title: Discovery of novel antiviral peptides using a WGAN-GP and BiLSTM-based hybrid model
sec.p: In the subsequent experiment, we identified virus-specific AVPs from the newly generated sequences produced by the WGAN-GP model using a previously developed BiLSTM-based prediction model. The newly generated peptides were applied to the BiLSTM model, which provided prediction probabilities for each sequence. Sequences with a prediction probability greater than or equal to 0.5 were classified as AVPs, whereas those with a probability below 0.5 were categorized as non-AVPs.

Table 2 provides a comprehensive summary of the AVPs generated for 12 distinct viral targets, showcasing the model’s ability to identify a diverse repertoire of peptide sequences with potential antiviral activity. We generated 300 unique sequences and evaluated their potential effects across 12 viral endpoints. Because individual sequences were predicted to act on multiple endpoints, they were included multiple times, corresponding to the endpoints they targeted. This overlap led to a total of 815 recorded entries, reflecting the multi-target potential of certain peptides. These findings highlight the ability of some peptides to act as broad-spectrum antivirals, underscoring their potential therapeutic value.

Influenza A virus (INFVA) emerged as the most prominent target, with 199 AVPs generated, reflecting the model’s exceptional performance in addressing influenza. Similarly, SARS coronavirus, dengue virus type 2 (DENV2), and hepatitis B virus (HBV) also exhibited substantial outputs, with 127, 86, and 86 AVPs, respectively, highlighting the model’s effectiveness in targeting these clinically significant viruses. In contrast, endpoints such as human parainfluenza virus 3 (HPIV3), which yielded only 4 AVPs, reveal areas of potential limitation, likely attributable to sparse data or reduced predictive efficiency. This distribution underscores the robustness of the model in generating AVPs for well-represented viral targets while highlighting the need for optimization to improve predictive power for underrepresented endpoints. sec.title: Local pairwise sequence alignment
sec.p: To assess the sequence similarity between the newly generated AVPs and known AVPs, we performed local pairwise sequence alignment using the Smith-Waterman algorithm. The similarity scores for each viral endpoint are presented in the histograms. The similarity scores were displayed between 0.0 and 1.0, with varying distributions across different viruses. The mean and median similarity scores are annotated for each viral target to provide a quantitative summary of the alignment results.

Figure 10 reveals that the close proximity of mean and median similarity values in many cases suggests symmetrical distributions for certain viruses, while marked asymmetries are evident in others. Notably, the highest mean and median similarity scores were observed for five key viruses: DENV2, RSV, HPIV3, SARS-CoV, and HBV. These viruses exhibited mean similarity values ranging from 0.44 to 0.51 and median values around 0.45 to 0.50, indicative of substantial sequence alignment between the generated peptides and known AVPs targeting these pathogens. These high scores suggest a conserved sequence architecture, potentially driven by structural or functional constraints. Of particular note, RSV exhibited a high similarity distribution with a mean score of 0.51, emphasizing its sequence conservation.

In contrast, viruses such as HCV, HSV1, and FIV showed lower similarity scores, with mean values between 0.31 and 0.38 and median values as low as 0.25 to 0.33. These results reflect greater sequence diversity, highlighting a potential challenge in designing broad-spectrum AVPs for these viruses. For other viruses, including IFVA and VACV, broader distributions were observed, with mean values ranging from 0.41 to 0.42 and median values around 0.40. This points to moderate similarity, accompanied by potential structural novelty in the peptide sequences generated.

This analysis underscores the intricate balance between sequence conservation and variability across viral species, offering valuable insights for designing targeted antiviral strategies. The observed variability in similarity scores highlights the WGAN-GP model’s ability to generate both sequences resembling known AVPs and potentially novel ones with unique properties. This capability expands the sequence space for therapeutic discovery, positioning the model as a powerful tool for antiviral research. Experimental validation remains essential to confirm the biological activity of these generated sequences.Fig. 10

sec.title: Refined analysis of conserved motifs in AVPs
sec.p:
Figure 11 presents the sequence logos representing the conserved motifs identified across the generated AVPs. Three distinct motifs were visualized, each exhibiting different levels of sequence conservation at specific positions. The height of the letters at each position corresponds to the degree of conservation, quantified in bits, where taller letters signify a higher level of conservation. This visualization effectively highlights key residues likely contributing to the structural and functional properties of the peptides.Fig. 11

Figure 11 A illustrates the sequence logo of the identified motif 1, emphasizing the critical amino acid composition that underpins the structure and function of AVPs. The motif demonstrates a strong preference for positively charged residues, prominently featuring arginine (R) at position 1 and lysine (K) at 15. Central positions (7 to 11) are enriched with hydrophobic residues, including isoleucine (I), cysteine (C), valine (V), and leucine (L), which likely contribute to the motif’s structural stability. Polar uncharged residues, such as serine (S), are distinctly present at position 12, while positions 2, 4, and 5 exhibit notable variability, accommodating residues like aspartic acid (D) and tryptophan (W).

The sequence logo analysis in Fig. 11B highlights critical characteristics of the identified motif 2. Highly conserved residues are evident, including threonine (T) at position 1, valine (V) at position 3, leucine (L) at position 5, methionine (M) at position 6, cysteine (C) at position 7, phenylalanine (F) at position 8, and serine (S) at positions 9, 12, and 15. Positions 3 to 7 are dominated by hydrophobic residues such as valine (V), leucine (L), methionine (M), cysteine (C), and phenylalanine (F), suggesting their role in structural stability or hydrophobic interactions. Uncharged polar residues like serine (S) and threonine (T) are prominently distributed, while negatively charged aspartic acid (D) residues at positions 2, 11, and 14 emphasize the importance of ionic interactions. The recurring presence of serine (S) and aspartic acid (D) between positions 9 and 15 delineates a potential functional interface, which may play a pivotal role in peptide activity or target recognition.

The sequence logo analysis highlights the conserved characteristics of motif 3, as shown in Fig. 11C. Strongly conserved residues, including alanine (A) at position 1, tryptophan (W) at position 2, phenylalanine (F) at position 4, glycine (G) at positions 5 and 9, and serine (S) at positions 5 and 13. Hydrophobic residues, such as alanine (A), tryptophan (W), phenylalanine (F), and valine (V), dominate positions 1, 2, 4, and 10, respectively. Polar residues, including serine (S) and glycine (G) are critical for peptide adaptability. Charged residues are less prominent, with aspartic acid (D) at position 3 being the primary charged residue. This limited presence of charged residues suggests that the motif relies primarily on a balance of hydrophobic and polar interactions for its activity.

In addition, to further assess the functional relevance of the generated motifs, we compared them against known peptide sequences in the DRAMP13 (http://dramp.cpu-bioinfor.org/) and dbAMP 3.049 (https://awi.cuhk.edu.cn/dbAMP/index.php). These are an open-access and manually curated databases that provide diverse annotations of AMPs, including a substantial collection of experimentally validated AVPs. The results revealed that Motif 1 is present in 8 known AVPs, Motif 2 in 6 peptides, and Motif 3 in 1 peptide. These findings indicate that the generated peptides do not merely reflect generic sequence patterns, but may also capture biologically meaningful features shared with experimentally validated AVPs. Details on peptide names, sequences, biological functions, and corresponding PubMed IDs are provided in the Supporting Information. This suggests that the proposed generative framework has the potential to produce peptides with plausible antiviral functionality, warranting further experimental validation in future studies.

sec.title: Drug-like properties and synthetic feasibility of the generated AVPs
sec.p: To estimate the drug-like potential of the generated AVP sequences, we evaluated six key physicochemical descriptors: molecular weight, net charge at physiological pH (7.4), GRAVY index, instability index, Boman index, and total hydrophobic ratio. These properties were chosen based on their established relevance to peptide design, including solubility, stability, and synthetic feasibility. Previous studies have shown that AMPs typically have a molecular weight ranging from 2 to 10 kDa, exhibit amphiphilic characteristics, and are generally positively charged at neutral or physiological pH conditions50. Notably, AMPs with molecular weight below 5 kDa have been widely investigated and demonstrated promising potential as alternatives to conventional antibiotics51,52. The net charge of a peptide is determined by the sum of the charges of all its ionizable groups at a specific pH. GRAVY is used to represent the hydrophobicity value of a peptide36. The instability index is calculated based on the dipeptide composition of the peptide sequence and the empirical observation of how different dipeptides affect protein stability53. Boman index is a measure of the peptide affinity for proteins and its ability to establish biological interactions54. The total hydrophobic ratio of a peptide refers to the percentage of hydrophobic amino acid residues in the sequence.

Furthermore, we assessed the synthetic feasibility of the most promising drug-like peptides using the PepSySco (Peptide Synthesis Score) tool (http://tools.iedb.org/pepsysco/)59. PepSySco estimates synthesis accessibility based on Fmoc-based solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), a widely used method that employs 9-fluorenylmethyloxycarbonyl (Fmoc) as a protecting group during peptide chain elongation. The tool provides a score between 0 and 1, with higher values indicating greater ease of synthesis. The number of peptides exhibiting drug-like properties and synthetic feasibility is summarized in Table 2. Detailed information on the top-ranked drug-like peptides and their corresponding PepSySco scores is provided in the Data and Software Availability section.

sec.p: In this analysis, we investigated the impact of sequence mutations on AVP characteristics. Starting from the data set of generated peptide sequences, we filtered those containing conserved motifs, resulting in three curated motif-specific subsets. To assess the functional impact of amino acid substitutions across these conserved regions, a systematic in silico saturation mutagenesis strategy was applied to each motif-containing sequence60. For every identified motif instance, each residue position was individually substituted with the remaining 19 canonical amino acids, thereby generating a comprehensive library of single-point variants. This approach enabled exhaustive coverage of all possible substitutions within conserved motifs.

Subsequent statistical analyses were performed to thoroughly evaluate the functional consequences of individual amino acid substitutions within conserved motifs. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Due to efficient replication, different transmission routes, high genetic variation, prevention of harmful activities of viruses is challenging problem. Furthermore, the emergence of drug resistance and the lack of effective therapeutics for many viral infections highlight the urgent need for innovative approaches to drug discovery and development to combat these global health threats effectively. For instance, emerging resistance to SARS-CoV-2 antivirals has been observed in vitro during transmission studies conducted in cell culture under varying doses of antiviral drugs. This resistance complicates treatment, as demonstrated by prior studies highlighting naturally occurring antiviral resistance mutations and reports of 3.2% of untreated individuals exhibiting emergent resistance mutations to nirmatrelvir62.

A comprehensive meta-analysis encompassing 136 studies, including data from 28,539 HIV-1-infected children across 52 countries, revealed a concerning prevalence of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR). The analysis showed resistance rates of 26.31% in untreated children and 74.16% in those undergoing treatment63. These findings underscore the persistent challenge posed by drug resistance in managing viral infections. In the case of dengue virus, no antiviral drugs have been approved for clinical use, leaving treatment limited to supportive care, including fluid replacement and analgesics64. Numerous antiviral candidates have failed to progress to clinical trials due to suboptimal physicochemical and pharmacokinetic properties. Notable candidates such as chloroquine, prednisolone, lovastatin, and celgosivir have been tested in clinical trials but did not achieve sufficient viremia reduction to provide significant therapeutic benefits65.

As a result, AVPs have emerged as a key focus in research, demonstrating significant promise as potential antiviral drugs. They exhibit remarkable capability in combating viruses by disrupting the viral capsid, directly suppressing viral activity, and interfering with different stages of the viral replication cycle66,67. Between 2000 and 2020, the number of FDA-approved AVP patents exhibited a consistent upward trend, reflecting significant advancements in peptide-based therapeutics. Notably, these patents demonstrated broad-spectrum antiviral efficacy, targeting high-priority pathogens such as HIV, Rift Valley Fever Virus (RVFV), influenza A and B, and the Ebola virus. Furthermore, specialized peptide-based antiviral treatments for HIV, influenza, and hepatitis garnered regulatory approval, underscoring the growing recognition of peptides as a pivotal class of antiviral agents10. The discovery of AVPs can be pursued through various advanced methodologies: (1) direct screening of natural sources, (2) rational design via computational strategies, and (3) high-throughput screening of extensive peptide libraries8. Particularly, in silico approaches have witnessed substantial progress, with cutting-edge generative deep learning technologies enabling significant breakthroughs and producing a growing number of successful AVP candidates68–70.

On these foundations, we have built a new framework by combining the advantages of WGAN-GP and BiLSTM neural networks in designing and classifying newly generated AVPs. This hybrid framework leverages the generative capabilities of WGAN-GP to create novel peptide sequences with potential antiviral properties, while the BiLSTM classifier ensures accurate prediction and validation of AVP activity. By integrating these complementary components, the approach not only enhances the diversity of generated peptides but also improves the reliability of AVP identification, offering a promising tool for advancing peptide-based antiviral research.

Consequently, the motifs identified in our study were systematically classified and demonstrated a distinct amino acid distribution, emphasizing their essential roles in mediating structural and functional interactions. Charged residues such as arginine (R), aspartic acid (D), and lysine (K) emerged as key contributors, likely facilitating ionic interactions and molecular recognition28,71. Meanwhile, hydrophobic residues, including cysteine (C), leucine (L), phenylalanine (F), tryptophan (W), isoleucine (I), valine (V), and alanine (A), were prevalent, emphasizing their importance in maintaining structural stability and interacting with hydrophobic environments. The presence of small residues, particularly glycine (G), was notable for enhancing the flexibility and adaptability of the motifs. Furthermore, the prominence of serine (S), a polar uncharged residue, suggested its role in hydrogen bonding and improving solubility28,71. Collectively, these findings highlight the significance of specific amino acid groups in shaping the functional properties of the analyzed motifs. Notably, permutation importance analysis identified phenylalanine (F), cysteine (C), leucine (L), isoleucine (I), and alanine (A) as the top five features driving the model’s predictive performance. Strikingly, all of these are hydrophobic residues. This result underscores the consistency observed across our experiments.

A detailed analysis of natural AVPs using databases such as the Antimicrobial Peptide Database (APD) has highlighted the amino acid preferences characteristic of well-known AVP families. Leucine (L) and cysteine (C) were identified as the most common hydrophobic residues, while lysine (K) and arginine (R) were predominant among charged amino acids. In the small amino acid group, glycine (G) was most frequently observed, and serine (S) was prominent in the polar group71. These findings reinforce the significance of our model in elucidating the amino acid patterns essential for designing and optimizing AVPs.

Additionally, viruses are categorized into two main types: non-enveloped and enveloped. Non-enveloped viruses feature a genome encased within a protein capsid, whereas enveloped viruses are surrounded by an additional viral membrane that encases the capsid or nucleoprotein core, consisting of both proteins and lipids72. In simpler terms, viruses are primarily composed of two essential components: the viral genome (which can be RNA or DNA) and a protein capsid encoded by the virus. If a virus contains only these two elements, it is classified as non-enveloped. On the other hand, if it possesses a lipid bilayer enveloping the capsid, it is classified as an enveloped virus73. In this investigation, all 12 viral endpoints were categorized as enveloped viruses, substantiated by data from prior virological studies74–85. Enveloped viruses pose significant global health challenges, as evidenced by recent outbreaks caused by SARS and COVID-19. Moreover, persistent infections by viruses such as HBV, HCV, and HIV continue to impact millions of individuals worldwide, underscoring the urgent need for innovative antiviral strategies. Research into combating enveloped viruses has become a critical priority to mitigate their extensive public health burden86. Hydrophobicity has emerged as a critical determinant in the antiviral activity of peptides targeting enveloped viruses6. The presence of hydrophobic residues plays a key role in stabilizing the structural core of the peptides and mediating interactions with the hydrophobic domains of viral components87. In this study, we identified essential hydrophobic amino acids derived from conserved sequence motifs within newly designed AVPs. These findings offer significant insights into the rational design of potent antiviral agents, advancing the development of therapeutics against enveloped viruses.

Furthermore, the inherent stability of the capsid and the scarcity of accessible targets pose considerable challenges in developing antiviral agents against non-enveloped viruses88. While AVPs have been predominantly effective against enveloped viruses, recent research suggests that cationic peptides may also exhibit activity against non-enveloped viruses. These peptides are characterized by their positive charge and amphipathic properties and incorporate cationic residues such as lysine (K) and arginine (R). Their mechanism of action involves disrupting or aggregating viral particles by targeting negatively charged components of the virus, including the capsid and other structural features89. Importantly, these findings highlight the potential applicability of our model in discovering AVPs effective against non-enveloped viruses, given the high conservation of lysine (K) and arginine (R) residues in the motifs identified within our newly developed AVPs.

Deep learning tools and peptide-related databases, particularly those focusing on antimicrobial and antiviral activities, have been rapidly expanding in recent years. One prominent example is dbAMP, a well-curated resource that offers in-depth information on AMPs, including their sequences, biological functions, physicochemical characteristics, and structural features. Moreover, it integrates several prediction tools related to AMPs and AVPs, such as activity prediction, hemolytic toxicity, and peptide half-life estimation49. These updates underscore the importance of considering multiple aspects in the rational design of therapeutic peptides. Notably, the database incorporates AVP-IFT, a state-of-the-art, two-stage deep learning-based predictor capable of identifying AVPs and characterizing their viral targets at both family and species levels24. This highlights the relevance of our study, which proposes a hybrid framework approach combining generative and predictive models to facilitate the discovery of therapeutic peptides targeting 12 distinct viral endpoints. With its robust predictive performance and deployable architecture, our framework positions itself as a valuable tool in the field of computational peptide design.

Recent advancements in deep learning-based peptide prediction have enabled the development of more sophisticated and interpretable architectures. For instance, ACP-CapsPred introduced an explainable capsule network framework for the identification and functional characterization of anticancer peptides (ACPs) across various cancer types90. While our model, built upon a recurrent neural network architecture (i.e. BiLSTM), achieved a prediction accuracy of 86.1% on AVP data sets, ACP-CapsPred leveraged a next-generation neural network (i.e capsule networks), demonstrating accuracies of 80.25% and 95.71% on different benchmark data sets. These findings collectively highlight the increasing promise of deep learning approaches in peptide discovery. Given that ACPs are a subclass of AMPs, which encompass AVPs, we consider that next-generation neural network architectures may also be applicable to AVP design and discovery.

While the present study offers a robust computational framework for the generation and evaluation of AVPs, translating these findings into practical applications will require further experimental investigation. Validation through wet-lab approaches, such as peptide synthesis followed by antiviral assays against specific viral strains, would help confirm their biological activity. Moreover, evaluating their toxicity and stability in relevant cell lines would provide additional insights into their therapeutic viability. Such experimental efforts will be essential for bridging the gap between in silico predictions and real-world clinical applications.

sec.title: Advantages and limitations
sec.p: The proposed research utilizing WGAN-GP and BiLSTM for AVP identification presents several notable scientific advantages. First, WGAN-GP ensures stable training dynamics and mitigates mode collapse, facilitating the generation of diverse and high-quality peptide candidates. Second, BiLSTM is particularly effective in capturing long-range dependencies within peptide sequences, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of amino acid interactions. Third, the integration of generative models with sequence-based deep learning approaches introduces a novel framework that surpasses traditional methodologies in peptide discovery. Finally, this approach demonstrates significant potential for real-world applications in drug discovery and the development of peptide-based therapeutics.

Despite its potential, the approach has some limitations. It requires a large, diverse data set for effective training, as insufficient data can lead to poor generalization. Both WGAN-GP and BiLSTM are computationally intensive, demanding significant computational resources and longer training times. Hyperparameter tuning is challenging due to the sensitivity of the models to parameters such as learning rate, batch size, or gradient penalty weight. Additionally, there is a potential risk of generating peptides that are mathematically consistent but lack biological relevance.

Moreover, one limitation of this study lies in the construction of the negative data set. As experimentally validated non-AVPs are extremely limited in current public databases, our negative samples were selected based on the absence of virus-specific activity annotations rather than empirical confirmation of inactivity. This approach, commonly adopted in previous studies, may lead to the inclusion of false negatives, referring to peptides that have uncharacterized antiviral activity but are incorrectly labeled as inactive due to the lack of annotation. To mitigate this limitation, we incorporated data from DBAASP25, a curated database that provides experimentally determined susceptibility testing results for peptides, including those found to be inactive. Despite this effort, the inherent uncertainty in negative labeling remains a challenge and may influence the model’s performance and generalizability.

sec.title: Future directions
sec.p: To advance the performance and broaden the applicability of the proposed methodology for identifying AVPs, several promising directions warrant further investigation. First, the integration of data augmentation techniques could significantly enhance the diversity and volume of the training data set, thereby improving the model’s generalization capabilities. Second, the adoption of ensemble learning strategies, such as combining BiLSTM with complementary architectures like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or Transformers, holds the potential to boost prediction accuracy and robustness by leveraging the strengths of diverse model architectures. Third, the implementation of an active learning framework, wherein the model iteratively selects the most uncertain peptide candidates for experimental validation, provides a strategic approach to prioritize high-value samples. This approach can effectively reduce experimental costs while accelerating the discovery of novel peptides. Fourth, future wet-lab validation, including peptide synthesis and antiviral assays, will be essential to confirm the biological relevance and therapeutic potential of the proposed candidates. Lastly, but no less important, subsequent studies should include experimentally validated inactive peptides as more data become available, as this is crucial for improving the reliability of predictive models. Collectively, these advancements aim to augment the predictive efficacy of the model and streamline the peptide discovery pipeline.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this study, we developed and tested a hybrid model combining Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks to generate and identify antiviral peptides across 12 viral endpoints. Our approach shows potential in addressing challenges like peptide sequence diversity and functional relevance while providing reasonable accuracy in classification tasks. By combining WGAN-GP’s ability to generate peptide sequences and BiLSTM’s strength in capturing sequence patterns, this model provides a useful tool for peptide-based drug research. This approach could support the discovery of new antiviral peptides and has the potential for broader applications in bioinformatics. Future efforts will aim to improve the model and explore its use with larger and more varied data sets.
